deep.reconstruction:
Context: E598 reworks Lagrange's theory of quadratic forms (the 'divisors' D of numbers p^2 ± n q^2, written as reduced forms f r^2 + 2g r s + h s^2) and compares it with Euler's own residue-class description: prime divisors lie in classes 4n·i + a. Example 11 (begun on p. 303) treats F = p^2 - 30 q^2, equivalently 30 p^2 - q^2, so n = 30 and the modulus is 120.

On p. 303 the reduction gives four kinds of divisor forms: r^2 - 30s^2, 2r^2 - 15s^2, 3r^2 - 10s^2 and 5r^2 - 6s^2. The g = 1 and g = 2 cases give nothing new, since 2r^2 + 4rs - 13s^2 = 2(r+s)^2 - 15s^2. Euler labels the four kinds D = F, 2D = F, 3D = F and 6D = F.

This page computes the admissible residues a modulo 120, taken up to sign, from the values of each form and of its 'affine' companion with the coefficients swapped.
- Square class: a = p^2 gives 1 and 49 coprime to 30.
- 30 - p^2: gives 29, 19, 91. Using 120 = 30·4, 120 - p^2 gives 119 and 71.
- 2t^2 - 15: gives 13, 7, 17, 83, 113, 107. Its companion 15p^2 - 2q^2 with p = 3, i.e. 135 - 2q^2, adds 103.
- 3t^2 - 10: gives 7, 17. Its companion 10t^2 - 3 adds 37.
- 5t^2 - 6: gives 1, 119. Its companion 6t^2 - 5 gives 1, 19, 49, 91.

Fifteen residues are found: 1, 7, 13, 17, 19, 29, 37, 49, 71, 83, 91, 103, 107, 113, 119. The required number is φ(120)/2 = 16. The set is closed under a → 120 - a, so the missing 101 = 120 - 19 is supplied. Modulo sign this leaves eight classes a = 1, 7, 13, 17, 19, 29, 37, 49. The eight complementary classes (11, 23, 31, 41, 43, 47, 53, 59) can never contain divisors.

In modern terms this is the set of units a mod 120 with Kronecker symbol (120/a) = +1: the kernel of the quadratic character attached to Q(√30).

§37 (Cor. 1): assuming Euler's 'theorem' (his form of quadratic reciprocity: every prime in an admissible class 4ni + a divides some p^2 ± nq^2), Euler lists the primes below 240 in these classes.

§38 (Cor. 2): the same residues come from different forms, so the four classes collapse to two. If 5D = F (equivalently 6D = F) then also D = F; if 3D = F then also 2D = F. So every prime divisor satisfies D = ±F or 2D = ±F. In modern terms:
- the narrow class group of discriminant 120 has four classes, represented by x^2 - 30y^2, -x^2 + 30y^2, 2x^2 - 15y^2, -2x^2 + 15y^2;
- 5x^2 - 6y^2 represents -1, so it lies in the class of -F; 6x^2 - 5y^2 represents 1;
- 3x^2 - 10y^2 represents 2 (at x = 2, y = 1), so it is equivalent to 2x^2 - 15y^2;
- identifying a form with its negative, as Euler does, leaves two classes.

§39 (Cor. 3) begins assigning the character 1 or 2 to each residue class. This is in effect a genus assignment: the residue class mod 120 determines which of the two sign-merged classes represents the prime.
errors: §37: the list of primes below 240 in the admissible classes omits 211 (≡ 91 ≡ -29 mod 120) and 239 (≡ 119 ≡ -1 mod 120). Both are prime and have (30/p) = +1. For 211: (2/211) = -1, (3/211) = -1, (5/211) = +1. For 239: all three symbols are +1. Both lie in classes Euler himself has just listed (91 and 119).
§37 lists 1 among the 'numeri primi'. This is harmless and follows Euler's habit of including the unit.

Minor: on p. 303 Euler labels the fourth kind '6D = F' although the form is 5r^2 - 6s^2. This is justified because 6(5r^2 - 6s^2) = 30r^2 - (6s)^2, which is of the form 30p^2 - q^2, i.e. -F. On this page he correctly writes '5D = F, sive etiam 6D = F'.

ideas.what: Determining the admissible residue classes mod 4n = 120 for prime divisors of p^2 - 30q^2 by evaluating each reduced divisor form and its coefficient-swapped companion. Completion uses the symmetry a ↔ 4n - a and the count φ(4n)/2.
ideas.modern_name: Kernel of the quadratic (Kronecker) character mod 120; quadratic reciprocity in Euler's residue-class formulation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (residue-class form of reciprocity, conjectured 1744-1783); proof by Gauss 1801
ideas.where_published: E164, E256 and E552 contain the 4ni + α criterion; E598 itself is a summary of these

ideas.what: Observation that different reduced forms yield the same residue classes, so that, up to sign, the four divisor classes of discriminant 120 merge into two (D = F or 2D = F).
ideas.modern_name: Form classes of discriminant 120 identified up to sign (narrow class number 4); one class per genus
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1775, Recherches d'arithmétique) for reduction; Gauss (1801) for genus theory and proper equivalence
ideas.where_published: Analogous merging remarks occur in other examples of E598; I do not know of an earlier Euler text with this specific case

ideas.what: Attaching to each admissible residue class a 'character' (1 or 2) that says which divisor form represents the primes in that class.
ideas.modern_name: Genus characters / assignment of genera to residue classes
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), with precursors in Lagrange and Legendre
ideas.where_published: E598 (this paper); similar tables appear in E552 and related late papers

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine worked example of Euler's well-known residue-class version of quadratic reciprocity, combined with Lagrange's reduction. The class merging is correct but standard; it is a precursor of genus theory, which the Euler and Gauss literature already discusses. The only finding is a small computational slip: 211 and 239 are omitted from the prime list.
transcription_corrections: The garbled fractions '(1?-pp)/?', '(?0-pp)/?', '(6?-pp)/?' are the alternate forms of a for the 2D, 3D and 6D classes (fractions of 30 - pp, or similar, over 2, 3 and 6). They cannot be read reliably from the scan, but Euler immediately rewrites them as a = 2tt - 15, 3tt - 10 and 5tt - 6.
In §37 the image reads 'admisso meo Theoremate'; the transcription's '4ni+a' and 'pp±nqq' match the image.
